translation:
...it is so. Das Kabirji says that the company of saints is the very best of all, while outward garb (the wearing of robes) is as trifling as hundreds of dew-drops. But if we properly heed the teaching of a saint, it wipes away the faults of millions of our sins.

God works in the world only through His devotee. Adhyaruji's own utterance on this is given below.

_Ghodli kar vina mande re vishva, pag vina sacharachar phire ||ghodli||
Ghodli mukh vina bole saar, lochan vina dekhe sahu ||ghodli||
Ghodli udar pakhe kare aahar, indi vina sukh bhogave ||ghodli||_ (Like a little horse, without hands He fashions the universe; without feet He moves through all that is moving and unmoving. Without a mouth He utters the finest words, and without eyes He sees everything. Without a stomach He takes food, and without senses He enjoys pleasure.)

The senses are this "little horse." In this way God has created the universe without hands. Without feet He can move everywhere, through the moving and the unmoving. Without a mouth He utters the finest words, and without eyes He can see everything. Without a stomach He eats food, and without senses He enjoys pleasure.

Just as God, being all-powerful, can do everything, so too the devotee can enjoy all pleasures without craving for them, and he can do so by resting his faith on the power of devotion to God.

_Kabir chakor bharose chandrake, jalta gale angaar.
Harijan maya khaat hai, dazhat nahi lagaar. ||4||_ (Trusting in the moon, the chakor bird swallows a burning ember; likewise the devotee of Hari partakes of maya, yet is not burnt in the least.)

Das Kabirji says that the chakor bird has firm faith in the coolness of the moon, and so it swallows even a burning coal without being scorched; likewise devotees too partake of maya, trusting in devotion to God, and yet they do not have to suffer the threefold afflictions and other such sorrows.

Trikamdas Gordhandas has written a kundali (a linked-verse composition) on the chatak bird:

_Samajhya jan sansarma, chup thai maun rahay.
Bole bijo thai jaso, samjhi chup rahay.
Samjhi chup rahay, vani par kabu karta.
Sahej samadhi janogh, dhumade bachka bharta.
Samjhel gurugam gaay, chakor chanch angarma.
Chup thai maun rahay, samajhya jan sansarma._ (Those who have truly understood remain silent in this world; speak, and one becomes something else — so, having understood, one stays quiet. Having understood, one stays quiet and holds one's speech in check; the multitude who understand attain effortless absorption, [while others merely] gulp at smoke. Those who have grasped the guru's teaching sing of it, as the chakor puts its beak into the burning coal; having understood, one stays silent in this world.)

Trikamdas says that people who have truly understood in this world become quiet and remain inactive, without giving voice to any kind of utterance, for if they were to stir up some other agitation it would lead only to harm — so, understanding this, they stay quiet. Understanding this, they withdraw within and keep their desires under check. But those who wish merely to observe a vow of silence (muni-vrat) without this natural, spontaneous one-pointedness are only laboring at a futile effort. Those, however, who have truly grasped the guru's teaching swallow the burning coal and its heat without fear, just as the chakor does — such people who have understood walk on trusting in the guru's command. Thus those who have truly understood in this world will live out their lives peacefully, free of [worldly] craving.

The chakor bird eats burning coals on the day of the full moon. Regarding this it is said:

_Lagi lagan chhute nahi, jibh chonch jari jaay.
Mitha kaha angarme, jahi chakor chabaay._ (Once a deep longing takes hold it does not let go, even if the tongue and beak get burnt. What sweetness is there, after all, in a burning coal, that the chakor should chew it?)

When there is intense longing for something, it cannot be given up, even if — as with the chakor — the tongue or beak gets burnt; whether it is tasty or not is of no concern. What sweetness could there be, after all, in the burning coal that the chakor goes for, that even though it gets scorched, it will not let go of it?

Those with single-minded devotion become absorbed in God alone and have no concern for anything else. As to what such devotion should be like, it is said:

_Chakoranam mathuranam tatha shubham, lakshananam dosh nirbhuktam dharya shri-nama-tatparaih. ||1||_ (One devoted to the holy Name should bear these faultless marks — the vow of the chatak, the gaze of the chakor, and the listening of the peacock.)

Like the chatak (a steadfast vow), like the chakor (meditation), and like the peacock (listening to the sound) — these faultless marks should be adopted by one devoted to the [divine] Name.

In separation from Sita, Ram wandered about the forest in great distress; seeing the forest birds calling out, His mind agitated, Ram said to the birds, "I am burning in separation," and cursed them: He told the cuckoo that her song would fall silent after spring. He told the deer and doe that when they mated, the hunter would kill them. He told the elephant and she-elephant that when they mated they would swoon for seven days. He told the peacock he would become impotent. He told the lion he would mate only once in his life. And He said to the chakwa and chakwi (the ruddy-shelduck pair):

_Chakwa chakwine kahe, thajo tamaro viyog.
Hu virahine dekhi kari, tame bhogvo chho bhog. ||8||_ (He said to the chakwa and chakwi: may separation come upon you too — for even seeing Me in separation, you go on enjoying your union.)

He said to the chakwa and chakwi that even though they saw Him in separation, they still enjoyed their union with one another; therefore they too would suffer separation.

Hearing this curse, all the birds and animals came seeking refuge, and He then softened it somewhat. To the cuckoo He gave her song only for the spring season. He said the deer and doe would be killed by the hunter only if they mated by day; the elephant and she-elephant would swoon for only two ghadis (about forty-eight minutes). He said the peacock's line would increase through tears. He said the chakwa and chakwi would be separated only at night. He said the lion would mate only once in his life.

_Kabir harijan aisa chahiye, udar samo ras leh.
Tame ganthe bandhasi, to jale pakhsu deh. ||5||_ (Kabir says: the devotee of Hari should be such that he takes only as much relish as fills his belly; if he ties up more than that for himself, his whole body will burn away.)

Das Kabirji says that a devotee should be such that he enjoys the taste of food only enough to sustain himself; but if he is tempted to hoard more than that, then he will be utterly destroyed, body and all — burnt away completely.

_Kabir parmeshwar te jan bades, taka kaha unmaan.
Hari maya aage dharai, sant rahe nivani._ (Kabir says: the devotee is even greater than God — what measure is there for this? Hari keeps maya before Himself, while the saint remains untouched by it.)

Das Kabirji says that the devotee is greater than God, and the measure of this is that God keeps maya present before the devotee, while the saint remains untouched by it.

Confirmation that Vasudevji and His devotees are one and the same in form — Divine Maya and the Ten Incarnations.

The devotee (harijan) is nirgun (attributeless) for the very reason that Vasudev too dwells in attributeless form within His devotees.

_Rup rekh kachhu vapu nahi, aise he Raghupati Raay.
Aise harijan Jivana, je naam nirmal jas gaay. ||1||_ (Raghupati Ray, the King, has no form, mark, or body at all — such too is the devotee, O Jivan, who sings the pure glory of His Name.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that just as King Ram has no shape or form of any kind, so too are His devotees, who sing the hymns and kirtans of the holy divine Name.

_Rup rekh jihi hai nahi, adhar dhari nahi deh.
Gagan mandalke vichme, nirkho purush videh._ (He who has no form or mark, who bears no body at all — behold that bodiless Being in the midst of the sky of the inner heavens.)

Das Kabirji says that the Supreme Being, the Paramatma, who has no form, shape, or kind whatsoever, who is bodiless, who has never taken on a body — behold that Lord in the empty sky of your inner soul.

In verse 61 of the Samagam, quoting Madri's words from the eleventh shlok of the Pandav Gita, the oneness of God and His devotees is described.

Madri Uvach (Madri speaks):

_Krishne rataah Krishnam anusmaranti ratrau cha Krishnam punarutthita ye,
te'bhinna-dehaah pravishanti Krishne havir yatha mantra-hutam hutasho. ||61||_ (Those devoted to Krishna remember Krishna at night, and on rising again remember Krishna; with bodies no longer distinct from Him, they enter into Krishna, as an oblation offered with mantras merges into the fire.)

Those who are in love with Krishna remember Lord Krishna at night, and the moment they rise, they remember Krishna again. Just as an oblation offered into the fire with mantras merges into that fire, so too they, becoming one in body with Him, enter into Krishna.

Explaining this shlok, the Samagam writes that the body of those who constantly remember Krishna is itself the body of God — there is no difference between them and God. Giving an example of this, it says that whatever we offer into fire itself becomes fire. Explaining this point, Revered Yadunath Maharaj writes in Lintiyu 38, page 14:

"There is an iron rod; when put into the fire it turns red. Now if you tell someone that fire is in this iron, he will say yes. Then tell him to separate the rod and the fire and show them apart — that is impossible. In the same way, it is also impossible to show Ram as separate from Kabir."

This chapter on the single-minded devotee comes roughly in the middle portion of the Samagam. In it, the divine Name "Ramkabir" given to us by Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj is presented here as the central theme. We become confused seeing the joining of the two names Ram and Kabir, and so the explanation of this has been given here at length; explaining it briefly, it is said that just as the devotee and God are both undivided, so too Ram and Kabir are one and the same — the Samagam gives two sakhis (couplets) on this.

_Kabir Ram Kabira ek hai, chinhe virla koy.
Antar mari kapatki, tathe dise doy. ||1||_ (Kabir says: Ram and Kabir are one, but only some rare one recognizes this; because a veil of deceit lies within, they appear to be two.)

Das Kabirji says that Ram and Kabir are indeed one and the same, but only a rare few can understand this mystery, because those whose inner heart has the veil of maya's illusion drawn over it feel that these are two separate beings.

_Kabir Ramkabira ek hai, kahan sunanko doy.
Do kari soi janai, jako sadguru mila na hoy. ||2||_ (Kabir says: Ram-Kabir is one; only in the speaking and hearing does it seem two. He who takes it to be two is one who has not met a true guru.)

Das Kabirji says that Ram and Kabir are one and undivided, but in speaking and hearing, for the sake of ordinary usage, their practical form appears as two, or as many; but only those who have not found a true guru take them to be two in ultimate reality.

Much has been said about the oneness of Ram and Kabir:

_Kabir Ram Kabira hoi rahya, kiyo kaljug mahi pravesh.
Sarv santan sukh karane, naam dharaya das doy._ (Kabir: Ram became Kabir and entered the Kali Yuga; for the well-being of all saints, He took on two names as devotee.)

Gyaniji Maharaj says in the Bhetka Ang that God, who bears the name Ram, became one in the form of Kabir and became known in the Kali Yuga as Ram-Kabir. To bring about the welfare of all saints, God took on these two forms — Ram-Kabir (Krishna-Kabir) — and assumed the title of being God's own devotee.

_Do aksharke antare, Ram Kabira ek.
So samjhat hai Jivana, jake sadguru diyo vivek._ (Only the two syllables differ — Ram and Kabir are one. This is understood, O Jivan, only by him to whom the true guru has given discernment.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that the only difference between Ram and Kabir is in these two sets of syllables. Otherwise, Ram and Kabir are one and the same form. But this can be understood only by those to whom the true guru has explained the mystery of this name and form.

_Ram Kabira ek hai, kahan sunanku doy.
Inme dushadha jo kare, maha narki hoy._ (Ram-Kabir is one; only in speaking and hearing does it seem two. Whoever creates doubt about this becomes the greatest of sinners.)

Das Kabirji says that the divine Name is a single reality; only in speaking and hearing does it seem like two. But whoever harbors doubt about this matter will be the greatest of sinners.

_Ram Kabira ek ai, ja ghatma pravesh.
Sharir dhare pan Jivana, adhar unka desh._ (Ram-Kabir is one, who entered this vessel [the body]; He takes on a body, O Jivan, yet His true realm is unsupported, beyond.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that Ram and Kabir are one and the same — it is that very Ram who entered into the body of Kabir (Ram dwells within every single body); God comes taking on a form with attributes, but God's true dwelling place is a unique one within the innermost self.

On this sakhi Trikamdas has written a kundali:

_Ram Kabira ek ai, ja ghatma pravesh.
Sharir dhare pan Jivana, adhar unka desh.
Adhar unoka desh, dekhe koi gurugam chela.
Manmati samajhat nahi, samje jene vivek hai.
Ja ghatnam pravesh, Ram Kabira ek hai._ (Ram-Kabir is one, who entered this vessel; He takes on a body, O Jivan, yet His true realm is unsupported, beyond. His unsupported realm — only a disciple who has received the guru's teaching can see it. One who follows his own opinion does not understand; only one with discernment understands. He who entered by name into this vessel — Ram and Kabir are one.)

Ram and Kabir are one and the same — it is that Ram who entered in body under the name of Kabir. This Ram-God does not, in fact, take on a body as one with attributes and form; rather, His dwelling place is a unique one within the innermost self. God's true abode rests on no support of any kind, and it can be understood only by those disciples who have received their guru's teaching. But those who are self-willed, who think according to their own whims, do not grasp this mystery — they are the sort of fools who cannot tell right from wrong. Those who can discern right from wrong understand that, for God, form-with-attributes and the formless-without-attributes are both one and the same — that God who has entered into the world of bodies is that very God, Ram-Kabir, one and undivided.

_Ram Kabira ek hai, naam dharaya doy.
Kahe Kabir do naam suni, bharam pado mat koy._ (Ram-Kabir is one; only two names have been taken on. Kabir says: hearing these two names, let no one fall into confusion.)

Das Kabirji says that Ram and Kabir are one and the same, but only two separate names have been taken on. Kabir says, let no one, on hearing two names, fall into the delusion that they are two separate beings.

_Virha virha sabko kahe, kachhu virhaka sidhaan.
Ram Kabira ek kare, Jivan jan pramaan._ (Everyone speaks of "separation, separation," but there is a true mark of separation. He who makes Ram and Kabir one, O Jivan, is proof of the true devotee.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that everyone keeps saying that the loving devotee is in separation from God, but the chief marks of a true virahi (one in longing) are these: just as Ram and Kabir are one and undivided, so too the true virahi is one who becomes wholly one in form with God.

Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj has given an important sakhi in the section on separation (viraha ang) about this. In it he tells what true separation is like: a person who is separated from his beloved is indeed a virahi, but through contemplation of the beloved he becomes suffused with that beloved and becomes one in form with him. It is said:

_Je jenu chintavan kare, te temaj thai jaay.
Prabhu chintavi prabhumaya thavu, kir bhramvat nyaay._ (Whoever contemplates something becomes exactly that; by contemplating the Lord, one becomes suffused with the Lord — as in the logic of the wasp and the caterpillar.)

Whoever keeps contemplating something becomes one in form with that very thing he contemplates. Therefore if we contemplate the Lord, we can become suffused with the Lord — just as when a wasp stings a caterpillar, the caterpillar keeps contemplating the wasp alone, and thereby itself becomes a wasp.

This is such a law — thus when Hanumanji met Sita in Lanka, Sita said that she was in separation from Ram, and what afflicted her more was that she contemplated Ram continually, night and day; therefore it would be well if, taking on Ram's own form, she became Ram's — for greater than becoming Ram himself is the joy of loving devotion found in becoming Ram's devotee. If she herself were to become Ram, how would she attain the joy of loving devotion to Ram? One can know the joy of sweetness only in eating sugar-candy; but if she herself became the sugar-candy, how could she know what taste is in it? In the same way, Jivanji's sakhi tells us that a true virahi is like Kabir: just as Kabir became one with Ram-Kabir, so too, if one becomes one in form with the very mark of separation, that one is reckoned a true virahi.

_Ram jape nit santko, sant jape nit Ram.
Gyani palak na visare, aama saama naam. ||2||_ (Ram forever recites the saint's name, and the saint forever recites Ram's; O Gyani, not for a moment do they forget each other's name.)

Gyaniji Maharaj says that Ram forever chants the name of the saint, and the saint forever chants the name of Ram. Thus the two never forget each other's names, not even for a single moment.

_Swami sevakme vase, sevak swami mahi.
Gyani dono mil rahya, palbhar visare nahi. ||3||_ (The Master dwells in the servant, and the servant in the Master; O Gyani, the two remain merged and never forget each other for even a moment.)

Gyaniji Maharaj says that God the Master dwells within the devotee, and the devotee dwells within God; thus the two have merged into one another. Not even for a moment do they forget each other.

_Ye yatha mam prapadyante tams tathaiva bhajamyaham,
mama vartma-anuvartante manushyah partha sarvashah. ||11||_ In whatever way they come to Me for refuge, in that same way do I bestow Myself upon them — that is, I grant them their fruit; to one who worships Me desiring worldly fruit, I show grace by granting the fruit he wishes, and to one who worships Me without desire, I give him My own abode. O Partha, in every way, men follow My path.

_Virha bauri Jivana, aatur haal sharir.
Ram Kabira jab milai, tab paavai man dhir._ (Separation drives one mad, O Jivan; the body remains in an anguished state — only when Ram and Kabir become one does the mind find peace.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that the restless condition of a body made distraught by the pain of separation is such that its mind finds peace only when it becomes one in form with the beloved.

_Ram Kabir hi satya hai, aur sat hi Ram Kabir.
Paramatma Parameshwar hai, vohi din bandhu Raghuvir._ (Ram-Kabir alone is the truth, and truth itself is Ram-Kabir; He is the Supreme Soul, the Supreme Lord — He alone is the friend of the lowly, Raghuvir.)

In the Bhet Sakhi it is said that there is no difference in Ram-Kabir; Ram-Kabir is itself the true, real divine reality, and that which is the ultimate truth, the Parabrahma, is itself Ram-Kabir. Thus Kabir's supreme, highest soul is the Supreme Lord — He, born among men, is Ram, the benevolent friend of His devotees.

_Kabir dekho Ram hai, ek hi ras bharpur.
Jaise urvase sab bana, chini sakkar gud._ (Kabir: behold, it is Ram in everything — one single essence, brimming full — just as from sugarcane are made sugar, sugar-candy, and jaggery.)

Das Kabirji says: reflect deeply and see — Ram alone dwells in everything. This one essence in the form of Ram is fully present and pervading in each and every thing; just as from sugarcane are made sugar, sugar-candy, and jaggery, so too from this one Ram has this whole universe come to be, in its many varied forms.

_Raat dhola pila hai, koi kala hai aur laal.
Ram prabhuke sabhi to, bhinna bhinna hai ye baal._ (Some are red, some white, some yellow, some black — all of these are the children of Lord Ram, differing only in outward form.)

In the Bhet Sakhi it is said that in this world some are red, some white, some yellow, and some black — all of these are indeed the varied children of Lord Ram.

_Ram Ram japte japte, Kabir Ram ho gaye.
Aur Kabir Kabir kahte kahte, Ram Kabir ban gaye._ (Chanting "Ram, Ram" again and again, Kabir became Ram; and saying "Kabir, Kabir" again and again, Ram became Kabir.)

In the Bhet Sakhi it is said that by chanting Ram's name, "Ram, Ram," Kabirji became Ram, and in the same way, by saying "Kabir, Kabir," Ram took on the form of Kabir.

_Mera man nirmal bhaya, jaisa chokkha nir.
Piche piche Hari phirat, japat Kabir Kabir._ (My mind became pure, like clear water; behind me Hari now wanders, chanting "Kabir, Kabir.")

Das Kabirji says that when my mind became free of defilement, like clear water, God began following behind me, chanting "Kabir, Kabir."

_Prem rup Kabirji, aatam Raghupati naam.
Jan tarveku Jivana, kali kiyo vishram._ (Kabirji is the very form of love; the Name of Raghupati is his soul; to ferry devotees across, O Jivan, he took his abode in the Kali Yuga.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that Kabirji is the very form of love, and the Name of Ram is his soul; in this form of Ram-Kabir, he came into the Kali Yuga in order to deliver His devotees.

_Kabir marte marte jag mua, sut vit daara joy.
Ram Kabira ho raha, yo mua, ek barabar boy._ (The world dies again and again, looking upon son, wealth, and wife; but he who has become Ram-Kabir dies in this manner — sowing as one and equal with God.)

Das Kabirji says that the worldly soul, looking on maya such as son, wealth, and wife, dies over and over in delusion. But the loving devotee soul who is of Ram's own form keeps an equal vision toward the one Ram present in all, becomes free of bodily pride, and becomes one in form with Ram.

_Ram-Krishna Karima ek hai, naam dharaya doy.
Kahai Kabir do naam suni, bharam pado mat koy._ (Ram-Krishna and Karim [the Merciful] are one; only two names have been taken on. Kabir says: hearing these two names, let no one fall into confusion.)

Das Kabirji says that Ram-Krishna and the merciful Khuda (God) are one and the same God, but only these two names have been taken on. There is no need for anyone to make a distinction between these two.

_Sahjai sahjai sab gaya, sut vit kaam nikaam.
Ekmek hai Ram mil raha, das Kabira Ram._ (Naturally, effortlessly, all passed away — desire for son, wealth, and worldly aims; utterly merged as one, Ram remains united [with him] — the servant Kabir is Ram.)

Das Kabirji says that when the state of natural spontaneity (sahaj) is attained, the desire for offspring, the desire to give away wealth, and worldly desire naturally fall away on their own, and the devotee, merging together with Ram, becomes one and the same with Him.

In the shlok on Hari it is said that Hari and His devotee are one — this shlok is from the Niranjan Purana:

_Vaishnava Vishnu-dehash cha bhinnam janati ye narah,
te narah narakam yanti yavash chandra-divakarau. ||62||_ Those who consider the Vaishnavas and the body of Lord Vishnu to be separate — such people fall into hell (suffering) for as long as the moon and sun exist.

_Vaishnava mam dehastu tasmat pujyo mahamune,
anyatnam parityajya Vaishnavan bhaja shashvatam._ O great sage, the Vaishnavas are Myself, My very body — therefore worship them alone. Give up all other endeavors and forever worship, serve, and keep the holy company of the Vaishnavas alone.

_Harih sada vasottatra yatra bhagavata janah,
gayanti bhakti-bhavena harer namaiva kevalam._ Wherever devotees sing only the Name of Hari with a spirit of devotion, there God dwells forever.

_Kabir Shankar puchhe Brahmaku, ek akshar tattva-saar.
Je te bhakt bhomi par, te te Hari avataar._ (Kabir: Shankar asks Brahma about the one imperishable essence of truth — whatever devotees there are upon this earth, they are all incarnations of Hari.)

Das Kabirji says that Shankar asks Brahma about the one imperishable divine reality, and this true thing is that however many devotees there are upon the earth, all of them are incarnations of God.

_Harijan mile to Hari mile, man paaya vishwas.
Harijan Harika ansh hai, jyon phulanme vaas._ (If one meets a devotee of Hari, it is as though one has met Hari — the mind gains this conviction; the devotee is a part of Hari, just as fragrance dwells in a flower.)

If one meets a devotee of Hari, it has instilled in the mind the conviction that one has met God Himself, because just as fragrance is itself a part of the flower, so too the devotee is a part of God Himself.

In the Bhaktamal, devotion, devotee, God, and guru — all four are said to be one and the same.

_Bhakti bhakt bhagwant guru, chatur naam vapu ek.
Inke pad vandan kiye, naasho vidhan anek._ Devotion, devotee, God, and guru — these four bearing different names have but one and the same body. By bowing at their feet, many obstacles are destroyed.

Dayaldas too has written likewise:

_Dayala Harigur, santko ek mel bai, jyu dudhi madhye maakh chhut chhash.
Yu Hari gur harijanme, tathe harijan Haridas. ||20||_ (O merciful Hari, guru, and saint are a single mixed union, just as within milk lie butter, ghee, and buttermilk; in this way Hari, guru, and His devotees are all in one another — hence the devotee is a servant of Hari.)

Dayaldas says that Hari, guru, and saint are one combined mixture. Just as butter, ghee, and buttermilk are all present within milk, so too Hari, the guru, and His devotee dwell within one another — and therefore devotees are the servants of God.

_Sadguru sadhu Ramji, naam teen ang ek.
Gyani jinche ang lahya, tin paaya bada vivek._ (Sadguru, saint, and Lord Ram — three names, one body. Whoever has grasped this, O Gyani, has attained the greatest discernment.)

Gyaniji Maharaj says that Sadguru, saint, and Lord Ram — these three names are different, but their body is one and the same. Those who have understood this mystery have understood the very best of all.

_Harithe harijan bade, samjhi dekhu man mahi.
Kabir sabgaj Haru vishe, so Hari harijan mahi._ (The devotee is greater than Hari — see this and understand it well in your mind; everything is contained within Hari, and so Hari is contained within the devotee.)

Das Kabirji says: take it firmly into your mind that the devotee is even greater than God, because that whole world which is contained within God is, in turn, contained within the devotee.

_Sant sangatme Hari vase, unte duri nahi.
Gyani sab jag thaapke, aap basa in mahi. ||4||_ (Hari dwells in the company of saints; there is no distance from them. O Gyani, having established the whole world, He Himself dwells within these saints.)

Gyaniji Maharaj says that God dwells in the company of saints and is not far from them; having brought forth the creation of the world while remaining beyond it, God Himself dwells within that saint.

_Garbhvant Govindadi, saheb santo mahi.
Gyani dije ekku, dono pokhya jaay. ||30||_ (Govind dwells [within, as one who is] pregnant — the Master is within the saints; O Gyani, give to the one saint, and both are nourished.)

Gyaniji Maharaj says that God dwells within the devotee as a child dwells in the womb; in this way God abides within the saints. Therefore if we give food and drink to the saint alone, God who dwells within that womb also receives nourishment from it.

_Mai anahadme had hu, mai nirgun gun mahi.
Mai Ramnaam samool hu, jan bina duja nahi. ||97||_ (I am the bounded within the boundless, I am both attributeless and possessed of attributes; I am wholly present in the Name of Ram — there is nothing else apart from My devotee.)

Das Kabirji says: within the boundless reality, I also abide as the bounded; though I am beyond the three gunas and free of attributes, I also possess attributes. I am wholly and entirely present in the Name of Ram; and apart from the devotee (harijan) in whom that Name of Ram dwells, there is nothing else.

_Hadme behad mil raha, behad e behadke mahi.
Pala gal paani bhaya, yu harijan Hari mahi. ||60||_ (The boundless merges within the bounded, and the bounded is within the boundless; as frost melts and becomes water, so too is the devotee within Hari.)

Das Kabirji, in the Asasa Ang, speaking of the furnishings kept in the house that is the universe, says that within the bounded limits of creation, the boundless divine reality lies merged and present. In that boundless reality it lies contained in its boundless state. Just as ice melts and becomes water, so too do devotees (harijans) abide within God.

_Sadhavo hridayam mahyam, sadhunam hridayam tvaham.
Madanyat te na jananti, naaham tebhyo managapi. ||68||_ O Durvasa, what more can I tell you — My loving devotees are My own heart, and I myself am the heart of these loving devotees. They know nothing apart from Me, and I too know nothing apart from them.

_Kabir dil mila dayalasu, tab kachhu antar nahi.
Pala gal paani bhaya, chu harijan hai Hari mahi._ (Kabir: when the heart merges with the merciful Lord, then no distinction remains; as frost melts and becomes water, so is the devotee within Hari.)

Das Kabirji says that if our inner heart merges with the merciful Supreme Soul, then no difference remains between us and God; just as ice melts and becomes water, so too the devotee merges within God.

In shlok 63 it is said that one who remembers the divine Name gains everything.

_Sarva-dharmarjita Vishnor naama-matraika-jalpika,
sukhena triptim aapnoti jagat-sarva-prakashika. ||63||_ One who gives up all other observances and chants only the Name of Vishnu attains satisfaction easily, with happiness.

In the commentary on this shlok it is said that by remembering the divine Name, the entire universe becomes satisfied; God is satisfied only by the taking of His Name, and if His Name is not taken, God is not satisfied. Giving an example of this it says that just as watering the trunk of a tree nourishes all its leaves, so too by taking the divine Name there is no need for anything else in the whole universe — no sacrifices, rituals, or mantras.

_Yatha taror-mula nishechanena, tripyanti tat-skandha bhujopashakhah.
Pranopaharaash cha yathendriyanam, tathaiva sarvahunam achyuta-ijya._ Naradji had told the Prachetas that just as watering the root of a tree satisfies its trunk, branches, sub-branches, fruit, and leaves, and just as taking food into the mouth satisfies all the senses, so too the worship of God accomplishes the worship of all.

_Yatha hi skandha shakhanam taror-mula nishechanena,
evam aradhanam Vishnoh sarveshaam atmanashchahi._ Just as the trunk and branches are satisfied by watering the root of the tree, so too, through worship of Vishnu, the worship of all souls is accomplished.

_Vyas na sadhan aur sab, Hari seva mastul.
Patrani patrani jal bhidyau, sinche taruvar mool._ (Vyas says: no other spiritual practice equals the service of Hari; watering leaf by leaf is like watering the root of the tree.)

Vyasdas says that no other spiritual practice equals devotion to God. Just as watering the root of a tree reaches every single leaf, so too devotion to God fully accomplishes every other spiritual practice.

_Vyas bhaktiko van dhanau, sant lage phal phool.
Patrani patrani jal bhiyai, taruvar shakha mool._ Devotion to Hari is the trunk of the tree; the saints are its fruit and flowers; the guru, saints, and devotees are its branches and leaves. By watering the tree of devotion to Hari with the water of loving devotion, these branches and leaves receive the water of loving devotion.

_Ek sadhai sab sadhai, sab sadhai sab jaay.
Mali sinchai moolko, phulai phalai adhaay._ (Accomplish the one, and all is accomplished; try to accomplish all separately, and all is lost. The gardener waters the root, and it flowers and fruits abundantly.)

Das Kabirji says that by practicing devotion to Hari alone, every kind of devotion is attained. But if we pursue misdirected worship here and there, all of it goes to waste — just as a gardener waters the root and thereby nourishes the flowers and fruit, but if instead of the trunk he waters only the leaves, all his labor goes to waste; likewise, without devotion to Vishnu, all other practices — sacrifices, rituals, yoga, chanting, and so on — go to waste.

_Pahile nikh mool sinchate, jal pahonche sab gair.
Gyani Ram sambharate, sadhan rahe na aur. ||21||_ (Water the root first, without fail, and the water reaches everywhere else; O Gyani, hold fast to Ram, and no other practice is needed.)

Gyaniji Maharaj says that by watering the tree's own root from the very start, the water reaches every part of the tree; in the same way, by remembering and chanting Ram, nothing else needs to be done.

Revered Yadunath, explaining this sakhi, writes in Lintiyu 6, page 22: to keep a tree alive there is no need to water leaf by leaf; by pouring water on the tree's root it reaches every place. In the same way there is no need to serve every deity — Ramkrishna is Himself the embodiment of all deities; serve Him alone.

Kabirji tells us to practice devotion in the right way:

(Kahera)

_Mool sinch man, mool sinch man, mool sinch man maari ho.
Moolke sinche phal phool laage, aise phale teri baari ho. ||1||_ (O my mind, water the root, water the root, water the root, my dear mind. By watering the root, fruit and flowers will come — thus will your garden bear fruit.)

_Phalke laage anahad gaaje, khul gai bharm phivari ho.
Panch pachiso nikar na aave, surat kare rakhwari ho. ||2||
Gagan mandal bich aasan kiya, trikuri lagi hai tari ho.
Kahe Kabir naamka kahera, mahrami hoy so vichare ho. ||3||_ (When fruit comes, the unstruck sound resounds, and the gate of delusion opens; the five elements and twenty-five constituents can no longer come near, for the inner awareness stands guard. He has made his seat in the sky of the inner heavens, absorbed in trance at the meeting-point of the three inner channels. Kabir says this song of the divine Name — only a true intimate of this secret will reflect upon it.)

O my dear mind, water with the water of loving devotion the true and rightful, original divine reality. By watering this root reality, you shall attain the flower of taking refuge in God and the fruit of the supreme abode — thus will your devotion come to fruition. When such fruit appears, the unstruck sound (anahad nad) will resound; the true experience of the divine reality will occur, and the gate of maya's doubts will be thrown open; all uncertainties will vanish. The tangle of the five great elements and the twenty-five constituents of nature will not come near you, and absorption in God's own nature will protect and save you from this material nature. Having laid out a seat for God in the sky of the inner soul, you shall become absorbed in the tri-kuti (the meeting point of the three inner channels, between the eyebrows). Kabirji says that only one who truly understands this boundless, immeasurable reality that is the divine Name will desire to remember and chant it.

For those who set aside true devotion and pursue misdirected worship, Kabirji says:

(Vasant)

_Dekho dekho re aa narki bhool, sinchat sakhane takhat mool. De. tek.
Pragat niranjan ghat samaan, tahe chhand nar puje pashaan.
Jal pive pashan ghoy, so to aad ant pashaan hoy. De. ||1||
Pag paatal jaka shish asmaan, so kaise sampoot samaan.
Alakh niranjan aave na jaay, so kaise diyo re tihaaro khaay. De. ||2||
Ehi bhaanti sab gayo bit, kaahu na maani shabd reet.
Kahet Kabir nar kiya na khoj, bhataki muva jaise banka rojh. De. ||3||_ (Look, look at this folly of hell — watering the branches while leaving the root and trunk dry. The manifest, spotless Lord dwells within this body; forsaking Him, man worships lifeless stone — he washes this stone idol and drinks the water used to wash its feet, and such a person is, from beginning to end, as dull as stone. He whose feet are in the netherworld and whose head is in the heavens — how can He be contained within your small vessel of stone? That imperceptible Lord neither comes nor goes — how then does He partake of the offering you give? In this way everything passes by, yet no one accepts the true teaching. Kabir says man has never set out to seek the true reality, and wanders lost in this world like the ignorant wild rojh, the forest antelope.)

Das Kabirji says: O brothers, just look and see what mistakes these human beings make. These people water the branches of the tree and give up watering its root. The manifest Lord is truly present within our own body, yet forsaking this true presence, people worship lifeless stone. They wash this stone image and then drink the water used to wash its feet — such people are, from beginning to end, as dull and insensate as stone itself. That Lord whose feet are in the netherworld and whose head is in the heavens — how could He be contained within your small vessel, in a piece of stone? That imperceptible, spotless Lord neither comes nor goes anywhere — how then could He eat the offering you give Him? Yet in such delusions everything has passed away, and still no one accepts my teaching. Kabirji says that people have not set out to search for the true reality — they wander about lost in this world, unaware, like the wild rojh (nilgai antelope) of the forest.

_Bhakte tushto Haristushto, harau tushtai cha devata.
Bhavanti siktaah shakhaash cha, taror mula nishechanaat._ If the devotee becomes satisfied, then God also becomes satisfied, and if God becomes satisfied, then the deities too become satisfied — just as when the root of a tree has been watered, its branches and twigs are watered by that too.

Kabirji has said that the manifest Lord dwells within the living human body during life; Jivanji's sakhi relating to this idea is given in the Samagam.

_Sant dware Jivana, sabka hoy sanmaan.
Raghupati jajante jug jajo, jap tap tirath daan. ||1||_ (At the door of the saint, O Jivan, everyone receives honor; worshipping Raghupati is to worship every merit of every age — chanting, austerity, pilgrimage, and charity.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that in the house of saints everyone receives honor and welcome; through devotion to Ram, service is rendered to the whole world. Whatever actions are performed in this world — chanting, austerity, vows, pilgrimage, charity, and so on — all of these accrue to the one who practices devotion to Ram.

Explaining this sakhi, the Samagam states that the dharma which Vaishnav devotees follow holds Ram-Krishna alone to be the true Supreme Lord; and when Sadguru Gopaldas met Jivanji Maharaj, he removed Jivanji's doubt as to what the divine reality is like — whether it is with attributes and form, or without attributes and formless — and gave the decision that the form of God as Morli Manohar (the enchanting flute-player) is indeed the true, rightful form of God, and that trying to understand God through His various incarnations is merely engaging with God's own maya. A pad (hymn) of Kabirji's on this is given: the visible incarnations are divine maya.

(Ashavari)

_Santo aavai jaay so maya, o pooran Brahma kalya hi kabahu.
O kahi gaya nahi aaya. ||1||_ (O saints, whatever comes and goes is maya; the perfect Brahma has never at any time been born — He has never gone anywhere, nor has He come.)
